pattern.title: Words ending in -sion

reading.title: Strange but True: Animals

passages.title: Koala fingerprints
passages.text: Koalas live in Australia and love hugging trees. Their fingerprints look almost the same as human fingerprints, even more alike than a chimpanzee's. Australian police were warned not to mix them up at a crime scene!

passages.title: The frozen wood frog
passages.text: In North America the wood frog freezes solid for up to 8 months. In winter its heart stops and its blood stops flowing. When spring comes, it thaws out and hops away.

passages.title: T. rex's closest relative
passages.text: Birds are the closest living relatives of dinosaurs. Scientists found substances inside T. rex fossils that match what is found in chickens, so the chicken is the dinosaur king's nearest modern relative.

passages.title: The Tudor shark
passages.text: Greenland sharks in the cold North Atlantic live for about 250 to 400 years. In 2007 one was found that might have been up to 512 years old, born around the time of Henry VIII. Nobody knows its exact age, so scientists say the age is estimated.

passages.title: Four identical babies
passages.text: The nine-banded armadillo from North America is the only vertebrate that always gives birth to four identical quadruplets. Scientists still don't know why.

passages.title: Pigeon maths
passages.text: Primates such as monkeys can think mathematically. Pigeons can too: they were trained to peck at groups of objects in order, 1, 2, 3, to earn a reward. That order is called a sequence.

passages.title: New legs for the axolotl
passages.text: The axolotl is a critically endangered amphibian from Mexico, a kind of salamander. If it loses a leg it simply grows a new one, and sometimes an extra one.

passages.title: Quick facts
passages.text: Baby elephants suck their trunks for comfort. Tigers have striped skin under their striped fur, and every tiger's stripes are unique. Flamingos eat with their heads upside down. All swans in England and Wales belong to the King. Female lions do 90 per cent of the hunting. One kind of jellyfish may live forever.

glossary: A cold-blooded animal with a backbone, like a frog, toad or newt. Babies have gills; adults breathe air.
Mammals with hands, hand-like feet and forward-facing eyes: monkeys, apes, lemurs.
Four babies born at the same time.
Worked out roughly, not measured exactly.

quiz.q: 1. How long does a wood frog freeze for each year? Tick one.
2. Complete the sentence: The fossils of a T. rex…
a: contain substances which are identical to those found in the chicken.
was found with an estimated age of up to 512 years.
has fingerprints that are almost identical to those of human beings.
enters a frozen state every winter.

quiz.q: 2. Complete the sentence: The wood frog…
a: enters a frozen state every winter.
was found with an estimated age of up to 512 years.
contain substances which are identical to those found in the chicken.
has fingerprints that are almost identical to those of human beings.
has fingerprints that are almost identical to those of human beings.
enters a frozen state every winter.
was found with an estimated age of up to 512 years.
contain substances which are identical to those found in the chicken.

quiz.q: 2. Complete the sentence: A Greenland shark…
a: was found with an estimated age of up to 512 years.
has fingerprints that are almost identical to those of human beings.
contain substances which are identical to those found in the chicken.
enters a frozen state every winter.

quiz.q: 3. Fill in the missing word: The nine-banded ______ from North America is the only vertebrate to consistently give birth to four identical quadruplets.
3. Fill in the missing word: …is the only vertebrate to consistently give birth to four identical ______.
4. Look at the section called Winged Mathematicians. Find the word which means ‘a particular order in which related things follow each other’.
5. What percentage of hunting is carried out by female lions?
Bonus: Which animal is the closest living relative of the T. rex?
Bonus: Which animal can grow a replacement limb?
Bonus: Who owns all of the swans in England and Wales?

open.q: 6. …a Greenland shark was found with an estimated age of up to 512 years. Explain why you think that the shark’s age is described as ‘estimated’.
open.starters: I think the age is described as ‘estimated’ because… / Scientists cannot know exactly because…
open.model: The age is estimated because scientists cannot know exactly how old the shark was. They worked it out roughly from clues, so it is a careful guess, not an exact number.

open.q: 7. Is it possible for something to still be alive since before the time of Henry VIII? Why do you think that the author has included this sentence in the text?
open.starters: The author has included this question to make the reader… / It makes you want to…
open.model: The author starts with a question to make the reader curious and want to read on. It makes you think about the answer and makes the fact about the very old shark more surprising.

open.q: 8. Which creature from the text did you find the most interesting? Give a reason for your answer.
open.starters: The creature I found the most interesting was the … because… / I was surprised that…
open.model: Any animal is a good answer if you give a reason from the text. For example: I found the axolotl most interesting because it can grow a new leg if it loses one, and even grow an extra one.

open.q: 9. Give one piece of evidence from the text which suggests that chickens are linked to dinosaurs.
open.starters: The text says that scientists found… / One piece of evidence is…
open.model: The text says that scientists found that the fossils of a Tyrannosaurus rex contained substances which are identical to those found in the chicken. This shows chickens are linked to dinosaurs.

maths.title: Maths Group 8 · Week 6
maths.intro: We are finishing the Addition and Subtraction unit: adding and subtracting big numbers with the column method, estimating by rounding, and solving word problems. On Friday there is a mixed times-tables test.

problems.title: Estimate, then calculate
problems.text: Use an estimation for each calculation, then calculate the actual answer.

parts.hint: Round each number to the nearest hundred or thousand first.
Round each number to the nearest hundred first.

problems.title: What could the calculation be?
problems.text:
a) Here is the estimation of an addition calculation: 2400 + 3200 = 5600. Write 2 different addition calculations it could be.
b) Here is the estimation of a subtraction calculation: 7600 − 2300 = 5300. Write 2 different subtraction calculations it could be.

parts.q: a) Two addition calculations that round to 2400 + 3200
parts.model: Any two sums where the first number rounds to 2400 and the second to 3200, for example 2381 + 3219 and 2449 + 3150.

parts.q: b) Two subtraction calculations that round to 7600 − 2300
parts.model: Any two subtractions where the first number rounds to 7600 and the second to 2300, for example 7612 − 2287 and 7550 − 2340.

problems.title: Is Tyreec right?
problems.text: Tyreec completed this calculation: 4517 + 3221 = 9738. Use estimation to show how you know that Tyreec is not correct.

parts.model: 4517 rounds to 4500 and 3221 rounds to 3200. 4500 + 3200 = 7700, which is much less than 9738, so Tyreec's answer is far too big. The real answer is 7738.

problems.title: The School Book Fair
problems.text: A school book fair sold 2,485 books on Monday and 1,768 books on Tuesday. The school had originally ordered 5,000 books for the fair.

parts.q: a) How many books were sold altogether on Monday and Tuesday?
b) How many books were left unsold?

problems.title: The School Trip
problems.text: A school is organising a trip for its students. There are 1,245 students in the school. On the first day, 368 students signed up for the trip. On the second day, another 457 students signed up.

parts.q: a) How many students signed up altogether?
b) How many students have not signed up yet?

problems.title: Planting Trees in Cyprus
problems.text: A community plans to plant 3,500 trees across several areas in Cyprus. In the first week, volunteers planted 1,275 trees. In the second week, they planted 968 trees. During a storm, 146 of the trees already planted were damaged and had to be removed.

parts.q: a) How many trees were planted in total before the storm?
b) How many trees remained after the damaged trees were removed?
c) How many more trees need to be planted to reach the original target of 3,500 healthy trees?
